extracted.intended_audience: poets and playwrights writing heroic/epic poetry and heroic drama; literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive criteria for composing heroic (epic) poems and heroic drama: what elements, style, structure, and stagecraft make a heroic poem or heroic play effective and noble. Includes guidance on use of supernatural elements, unity of action, character treatment, spectacle, and relation to historic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (one entire and great action)
rubrics_metrics.description: A heroic poem ought to be 'one entire and great action' — an entire, unified subject of sufficient magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the ancients' law of unity: center the work on a single grand action that gives the poem coherence. Avoid fragmenting the poem into disconnected smaller incidents that dilute the central purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Populate and vary the poem (persons, characters, accidents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem should be 'filled with persons, beautified with characters, and varied with accidents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include vivid, differentiated characters and a variety of incidents to sustain interest and to suit the greatness of the heroic form. Do not leave the poem scant in images or design relative to its majestic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevated style and liberty of fancy
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of an heroic poem raise ordinary poetic laws to a greater height and 'indulge... a farther liberty of fancy,' drawing things far above ordinary stage/prose proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a lofty, majestic tone and allow the imagination freer scope than in common or domestic subjects. Avoid confining expression to everyday diction and small-scale affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of supernatural/enthusiastic elements (gods, spirits, prophecy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ministry of the gods, the precipitation of the soul, and the fury of a prophet — the enthusiastic, supernatural parts — compose the most noble parts of epic poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate deities, spirits, or magical/spectral phenomena when appropriate: they are traditional and enrich the poem's grandeur. The absence of such ministry (as in Lucan) risks making verse too much like mere history or philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prosaic historical treatment and overly crowded sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not 'comprehend' deeds into verse as a mere historian or crowd sentences with epigrammatic points (a fault imputed to Lucan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist turning epic into a literal retelling of history or a string of pointed epigrams. Preserve the dignity and stateliness of epic diction rather than compressing thought into epigram-like stings or excessive rhetorical points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom from strict probability — allowance for improbability
rubrics_metrics.description: A heroic poet is 'not tied to a bare representation of what is true, or exceeding probable'; visionary or improbable objects are permitted if they rest upon some foundation (e.g., common belief in spirits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improbable events and visions are acceptable in service of imagination and grandeur so long as they are not impossible and have some cultural or narrative grounding. The poet needn't slavishly adhere to strict realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic authority on metaphysical/visionary subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets, guided by fancy, often explicate questions about spirits and separated beings better than philosophers or divines, and such poetical speculation is legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat metaphysical or supernatural themes poetically rather than demanding philosophical proof; rely on imaginative exposition as a valid approach to such topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage spectacle and theatrical devices (drums, trumpets, battles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Warlike instruments and representations of fighting on stage (drums, trumpets, battles) are necessary to produce the effects of an heroic play and to persuade the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use theatrical spectacle deliberately to raise the audience's imagination and make stage action persuasive. Employ sound and visual effects when they enhance the intended heroic impact, regardless of low-brow associations those devices may have.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's effort to dominate spectator imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should endeavour 'an absolute dominion over the minds of the spectators'; help the audience's fancy to deceive itself for the play's duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose and stage the poem so that the audience is convinced and emotionally engaged; aid their imagination with craft, pacing, and spectacle to achieve immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroes as great but human (allow human passions and frailties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroes should be men of honour and great spirit, but not divested entirely of human passions and frailties; they may act with imperfection (e.g., Achilles, Rinaldo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray heroic figures with grandeur and elevated virtues while retaining believable human emotions and faults. Avoid making heroes unrealistically scrupulous in a 'French' point-of-honour sense—greatness often coexists with passion and temper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow daring or apparently improbable deeds when plausibly motivated
rubrics_metrics.description: Bold, extraordinary actions (e.g., calming a mutiny, extraordinary single-person feats) may seem improbable but are not impossible and can be justified by character, reputation, daring, or historical precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting daring feats, ground them in the character's established reputation, circumstances, or plausible precedent rather than presenting them as gratuitous impossibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reject effective devices because of their provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not forbear an approved device simply because mountebanks or inferior practitioners have used it; effectiveness justifies use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate techniques by their efficacy for producing the intended effect, not by the social status of prior users. Adopt tried theatrical or poetic devices if they serve the poem's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model heroic plays on epic rules where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: A heroic play can legitimately be modelled by the rules of an heroic poem (Dryden models his heroic plays by epic rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider epic conventions (grand scale, mythic/supernatural elements, elevated diction) when composing heroic drama; the epic model can enrich dramatic form. Note: some (e.g., Cowley) argue instead for a more familiar, dramatic imitation—be aware of differing schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between dramatic familiarity and epic grandeur (contrasting view)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative view (advocated by some) is that heroic poetry should be 'dressed in a more familiar and easy shape' and 'more like a glass of nature,' resembling common actions and passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious of the tension between epic elevation and dramatic naturalism. If choosing a more familiar, practicable approach, aim for clear portrayals of ordinary passions and plausible virtues while recognizing that this yields a different aesthetic than the high heroic mode.
